title: Giving Interpretability Probes a Socket to Plug Into
hook: Probes and SAEs can see a jailbreak forming inside the model, but each ships its own calibration and glue code. LMSM borrows Linux Security Modules' shape: pluggable backends, one enforcement path.
key_points: Interpretability tools expose model-internal signals along the generation path, but a signal is not a security control.
Today each new artifact arrives with its own calibration, policy logic, and intervention code — integration work instead of a shared defense.

LMSM splits the problem three ways: a security backend supplies calibrated evidence, a versioned policy evaluates rules over trusted per-request context, and a separate gate authorizes release of buffered output.
That separation distinguishes mediation correctness from policy effectiveness, so rules or backends can change without touching request handling.
The prototype runs on Hugging Face Transformers and continuously batched vLLM, hosting SAE, transcoder, and dense-probe backends on one substrate.

On Qwen3-4B, LMSM-Checkpoint cut HarmBench attack success from 39.20% to 3.32%; XSTest false refusals rose from 2.40% to 4.40% and throughput held at 98.14% of an unmonitored path at 32 active sequences.
content_html: Layered defenses around a deployed LLM still get talked past. Interpretability research offers a tempting complement: sparse autoencoders, transcoders, and linear probes can read internal signals as the model generates, sometimes catching a harmful trajectory before the tokens are out. But a signal is not a control. In practice each such artifact arrives with its own thresholding, its own policy code, and its own way of intervening — so the tenth probe is as much work as the first, and none of them reinforce each other.
extra_html:
Borrowing a kernel's separation of concerns

Zhang and colleagues take the structure of Linux Security Modules and apply it to LLM serving. In Language Model Security Modules, a selected backend's only job is to expose calibrated evidence; a versioned policy evaluates active rules against trusted per-request context; and a distinct gate decides whether buffered output may be released. The point of the split is that mediation correctness — did every request actually get checked, under scheduler churn and continuous batching — becomes a separate question from whether the rules are any good.

The prototype covers both Hugging Face Transformers and continuously batched vLLM, and hosts SAE, transcoder, and task-fitted dense-probe backends on the same substrate, composing multiple rules per request. On Qwen3-4B, the authors report HarmBench attack success dropping from 39.20% to 3.32% with false refusals on XSTest rising from 2.40% to 4.40%, and 98.14% of the throughput of a matched no-monitoring path at 32 active sequences. The contribution is less a new detector than a place to put the detectors interpretability keeps producing.

related.title: Internal-State Probes Read the Situation, Not the Action
related.hook: Probes that seem to detect an LLM's harmful intent before it acts mostly just detect the prompt's topic — three careful tests find they don't predict future misbehavior.

related.title: SAE Interventions Are Unreliable
related.hook: Clamping a 'harmful' sparse-autoencoder feature looks like it stops bad behavior — but this paper recovers it 95.8% of the time, exposing the gap between feature-level and real control.

related.title: Scaling and Evaluating Sparse Autoencoders
related.hook: Tuning the sparsity penalty on an autoencoder is fiddly. Use a top-k constraint instead and you can dial sparsity directly — and scale SAEs to GPT-4.

flashcards.prompt: What are the three separated components in LMSM's design?

choices.text: A backend producing calibrated evidence, a versioned policy over trusted per-request context, and a gate authorizing output release
A prompt classifier, a fine-tuned refusal head, and an output-rewriting model
A red-team generator, a reward model, and a preference-optimization loop
A per-request sandbox, a rate limiter, and an audit log

flashcards.explanation_html: The split mirrors Linux Security Modules: evidence, policy, and enforcement are distinct, which is what lets a backend or rule change without rebuilding request handling.
